summary: Chino sits on nearly 30 square miles of the western Inland Empire's old dairy flats — and while most of those dairy operations have yielded to subdivisions and distribution centers, the city still carries a faint agricultural edge that separates it from the generic stucco-and-strip-mall suburbs nearby. The terrain is remarkably flat, with open-sky horizons to the south and east and the San Gabriel Mountains filling the northern skyline, which means winter sunsets behind those peaks can be genuinely dramatic. Chino's economy leans heavily on logistics and warehousing — its position along the 60 and 71 freeways makes it a hub for goods movement — so it functions as both a bedroom community for Orange County and Los Angeles commuters and a local job center, though commute corridors toward the coast can be brutal during peak hours. At a median income of roughly $104K against a median home price around $642K, the price-to-income ratio lands near 6.2:1 — tight but less punishing than coastal neighbors, with rent at $2,208 absorbing about 25% of gross median income. The city averages 9.5 hours of daily sunshine and a comfortable 65°F annual mean, making the 78°F daytime highs feel dry and manageable rather than oppressive. Chino is a place where affordable square footage and warehouse-economy paychecks coexist with long freeway commutes — a trade that defines much of the Inland Empire, compressed here into a single zip code.
